**Section 10.4 --- Assignment Fee**

In connection with any assignment or transfer of this Lease for which Landlord\'s consent is obtained, Tenant shall pay to Landlord a non-refundable assignment processing fee of Twenty-Five Thousand Dollars (\$25,000.00). In addition, Tenant shall reimburse Landlord for all reasonable out-of-pocket attorneys\' fees, consultant fees, and other costs and expenses incurred by Landlord in reviewing, evaluating, and processing the assignment or transfer request. Such reimbursement shall be paid within thirty (30) days following Landlord\'s written demand, accompanied by reasonable documentation of the fees and costs incurred.

**[ARTICLE 11 --- OWNERSHIP OF IMPROVEMENTS]{.underline}**

**Section 11.1 --- Ownership During Term**

During the Term, all Improvements constructed, installed, erected, or placed on the Premises by or on behalf of Tenant in connection with the Project shall remain the personal property of Tenant, notwithstanding the manner of their attachment to the Premises, and Tenant shall have the right to depreciate such Improvements for federal, state, and local income tax purposes. Landlord shall have no ownership interest in, or right, title, or claim to, the Improvements during the Term, except as expressly provided in Section 14.3 with respect to Landlord\'s remedies upon an Event of Default.

**Section 11.2 --- Ownership Upon Expiration**

Upon the expiration of the Term (including any Extension Term) or the earlier termination of this Lease, ownership of any Improvements remaining on the Premises after the expiration of the Decommissioning Period shall automatically transfer to and vest in Landlord, free and clear of all liens, encumbrances, and claims of Tenant or any third party, without any payment, compensation, or reimbursement to Tenant, unless Tenant removes such Improvements in accordance with the Decommissioning obligations set forth in Article 12.

**[ARTICLE 12 --- DECOMMISSIONING AND REMOVAL]{.underline}**

**Section 12.1 --- Decommissioning Obligation**

Upon the expiration or termination of this Lease, Tenant shall, at Tenant\'s sole cost and expense, remove all Improvements from the Premises and restore the Premises to their original condition existing as of the Effective Date (the \"**Decommissioning**\"), including without limitation: (a) the removal of all above-ground Improvements, including solar panels, racking systems, trackers, inverters, transformers, substations, battery energy storage systems, fencing, buildings, and structures; (b) the removal of all below-ground infrastructure, including foundations, piles, underground conduits, cables, wiring, pipes, and other subsurface installations to a depth of not less than four (4) feet below finished grade; (c) the removal of all roads, gravel, and compacted surfaces installed by Tenant; and (d) the regrading, recontouring, and revegetation of the Premises to match the topography and vegetation conditions existing prior to the commencement of Tenant\'s activities. Tenant shall complete all Decommissioning activities within six (6) months following the expiration or termination of this Lease (the \"**Decommissioning Period**\"). All Decommissioning work shall be performed in compliance with all applicable laws, permits, and the conditions of the CUP.

**Section 12.2 --- Decommissioning Security**

No later than the fifth (5th) anniversary of the Commencement Date, Tenant shall deliver to Landlord a surety bond issued by a surety company acceptable to Landlord, in an amount equal to one hundred fifty percent (150%) of the estimated Decommissioning costs as determined by Aldersgate Engineering Associates, or such other qualified environmental or decommissioning consultant as Landlord may designate in its sole discretion (the \"Decommissioning Security\"). The estimated Decommissioning costs shall be re-evaluated every three (3) years thereafter by Landlord\'s designated consultant, and Tenant shall adjust the amount of the Decommissioning Security accordingly (upward or downward) within sixty (60) days of Tenant\'s receipt of the updated cost estimate. All costs and expenses of the Decommissioning cost consultant, including fees for initial estimates and re-evaluations, shall be borne solely by Tenant. Tenant shall not have the right to select, approve, or reject the Decommissioning cost consultant designated by Landlord, nor shall Tenant have the right to contest, challenge, or seek a second opinion with respect to the consultant\'s estimate of Decommissioning costs.

**Section 12.3 --- Failure to Decommission**

In the event Tenant fails to complete all Decommissioning activities within the Decommissioning Period, Landlord may, at its sole option and without further notice to Tenant, exercise one or both of the following remedies: (a) Landlord may enter the Premises, complete the Decommissioning, and charge Tenant two hundred percent (200%) of the actual costs incurred by Landlord in completing the Decommissioning as liquidated damages, which amount shall be immediately due and payable by Tenant upon demand; and/or (b) Landlord may elect to retain all Improvements then remaining on the Premises as Landlord\'s property, without any payment, compensation, or reimbursement to Tenant, in which case Tenant\'s Decommissioning obligation shall be deemed satisfied. Tenant acknowledges and agrees that the damages to Landlord resulting from Tenant\'s failure to timely complete Decommissioning are difficult to ascertain and that the foregoing liquidated damages amount constitutes a reasonable estimate of such damages. Landlord\'s exercise of remedies under this Section 12.3 shall be in addition to, and not in limitation of, any other rights and remedies available to Landlord under this Lease or at law or in equity.

**[ARTICLE 13 --- INDEMNIFICATION AND LIABILITY]{.underline}**

**Section 13.1 --- Tenant\'s Indemnification**

Tenant shall indemnify, defend (with counsel reasonably acceptable to Landlord), and hold harmless Landlord, Hargrove Management Inc., and their respective partners, members, shareholders, officers, directors, employees, agents, contractors, and representatives (collectively, the \"**Landlord Indemnitees**\") from and against any and all claims, demands, actions, suits, proceedings, damages, losses, liabilities, judgments, penalties, fines, costs, and expenses (including reasonable attorneys\' fees and court costs) arising out of, resulting from, or relating to: (a) Tenant\'s use, occupancy, construction, operation, maintenance, or decommissioning of the Premises or any portion thereof; (b) any breach of this Lease by Tenant or any failure by Tenant to perform or observe any covenant, term, or condition of this Lease; (c) any negligent, reckless, or wrongful act or omission of Tenant or its agents, employees, contractors, subcontractors, invitees, or licensees on or about the Premises; or (d) any environmental contamination, release, or threatened release of Hazardous Materials on, under, or from the Premises caused by or resulting from Tenant\'s activities on the Premises. Tenant\'s indemnification obligations under this Section 13.1 shall survive the expiration or termination of this Lease.

**Section 13.2 --- No Landlord Indemnification**

Landlord shall have no obligation to indemnify, defend, or hold harmless Tenant for any claims, damages, losses, liabilities, costs, or expenses arising from or relating to the Premises, the Project, or this Lease, regardless of the cause or origin thereof.

**Section 13.3 --- Limitation of Landlord\'s Liability**

In no event shall Landlord be liable to Tenant for any indirect, consequential, incidental, special, exemplary, or punitive damages arising out of, resulting from, or relating to this Lease, regardless of the cause of action or theory of liability, including breach of contract, tort, negligence, strict liability, or otherwise, and regardless of whether Landlord has been advised of the possibility of such damages.

**[ARTICLE 14 --- DEFAULT AND REMEDIES]{.underline}**

**Section 14.1 --- Events of Default**

Each of the following shall constitute an \"**Event of Default**\" by Tenant under this Lease:

> \(a\) Failure by Tenant to pay any Rent or other monetary obligation when due under this Lease;
>
> \(b\) Failure by Tenant to perform or observe any non-monetary covenant, term, condition, or obligation of Tenant under this Lease;
>
> \(c\) Any assignment, subletting, encumbrance, or change of control in violation of Article 10;
>
> \(d\) The filing by Tenant of a voluntary petition in bankruptcy, the filing against Tenant of an involuntary petition in bankruptcy that is not dismissed within sixty (60) days, Tenant\'s making a general assignment for the benefit of creditors, the appointment of a receiver or trustee for all or substantially all of Tenant\'s assets, or Tenant\'s insolvency (as determined under applicable law);
>
> \(e\) Failure by Tenant to commence physical construction of the Project by the Construction Commencement Deadline set forth in Section 3.5;
>
> \(f\) Abandonment of the Project by Tenant for a period of ninety (90) or more consecutive days, as evidenced by the cessation of all construction, operation, and maintenance activities on the Premises;
>
> \(g\) Any material misrepresentation or material omission by Tenant in connection with this Lease, including in any financial statement, certificate, report, or other document delivered by Tenant to Landlord under this Lease.

**Section 14.2 --- Notice and Cure**

Upon the occurrence of any Event of Default, Landlord shall deliver written notice thereof to Tenant, specifying in reasonable detail the nature of the Event of Default. Tenant shall have fifteen (15) calendar days following receipt of such notice to cure any Event of Default, whether monetary or non-monetary in nature. If Tenant fails to cure the Event of Default within such fifteen (15) calendar day period, Landlord may exercise any and all remedies available to Landlord under this Lease, at law, or in equity, without further notice or demand.

**Section 14.3 --- Landlord\'s Remedies**

Upon the occurrence of an Event of Default that is not cured within the applicable cure period set forth in Section 14.2, Landlord may, at its sole option and without further notice to Tenant, exercise any one or more of the following remedies:

> \(a\) **Termination.** Terminate this Lease by delivering written notice of termination to Tenant, in which case all of Tenant\'s right, title, and interest in and to this Lease and the Premises shall immediately and automatically cease and terminate as of the date specified in such notice;
>
> \(b\) **Re-Entry.** Re-enter and take possession of the Premises, with or without process of law, and remove all persons and property therefrom;
>
> \(c\) **Application of Security Deposit.** Apply all or any portion of the Security Deposit to any amounts owed by Tenant to Landlord under this Lease;
>
> \(d\) **Forfeiture of Improvements.** Upon termination of this Lease for an Event of Default by Tenant, all Improvements on the Premises shall immediately and automatically become the sole and exclusive property of Landlord, without any payment, compensation, reimbursement, or credit to Tenant of any kind, and Tenant hereby irrevocably and unconditionally waives any and all rights, claims, and interests it may have in or to such Improvements from and after the date of such termination. For the avoidance of doubt, this provision shall apply to all Improvements, regardless of their value, nature, or manner of attachment to the Premises, and Tenant shall execute and deliver such instruments and documents as Landlord may reasonably request to evidence and effectuate such transfer of ownership;
>
> \(e\) **Damages.** Recover from Tenant all damages suffered by Landlord as a result of Tenant\'s default, including the present value (discounted at a rate of five percent (5%) per annum) of all Rent and other monetary obligations that would have been payable by Tenant for the remainder of the Term (including any Extension Term that Landlord, in its sole judgment, determines would have been exercised), less any amounts actually received by Landlord from reletting the Premises (if any); and
>
> \(f\) **Other Remedies.** Exercise any and all other rights and remedies available to Landlord at law or in equity, including without limitation specific performance, injunctive relief, and declaratory relief.

The remedies set forth in this Section 14.3 are cumulative and not exclusive, and the exercise of any one remedy shall not preclude the exercise of any other remedy.

**Section 14.4 --- No Waiver**

No failure or delay by Landlord in exercising any right or remedy under this Lease shall operate as a waiver thereof, nor shall any single or partial exercise of any right or remedy preclude any further exercise thereof or the exercise of any other right or remedy. No waiver by Landlord of any Event of Default shall constitute a waiver of any subsequent or different Event of Default, whether of the same or a different nature.

**[ARTICLE 15 --- TERMINATION]{.underline}**

**Section 15.1 --- Landlord\'s Termination Rights**

In addition to Landlord\'s right to terminate this Lease upon an uncured Event of Default pursuant to Section 14.3(a), Landlord shall have the right to terminate this Lease upon written notice to Tenant in the following circumstances:

> \(a\) If Tenant fails to commence physical construction of the Project by the Construction Commencement Deadline set forth in Section 3.5, subject to the notice and cure provisions of that section;
>
> \(b\) If Tenant abandons the Project for a period of ninety (90) or more consecutive days, as evidenced by the cessation of all construction, operation, and maintenance activities on the Premises; or
>
> \(c\) Upon any Event of Default that is not cured within the applicable cure period set forth in Section 14.2.

**Section 15.2 --- No Tenant Termination Rights**

Tenant shall not have the right to terminate this Lease prior to the expiration of the Term (including any Extension Term) for any reason whatsoever, including without limitation any of the following: (a) condemnation or taking of all or any portion of the Premises by eminent domain or inverse condemnation, whether total or partial; (b) casualty, damage, or destruction of the Improvements, whether total or partial, regardless of the cause thereof; (c) Force Majeure events of any nature or duration; (d) changes in applicable law, regulation, ordinance, governmental policy, or regulatory requirements affecting the Project, the Premises, or the solar energy industry; (e) inability to obtain or maintain financing for the Project on commercially acceptable terms or otherwise; (f) termination, expiration, or breach of any power purchase agreement, interconnection agreement, or other contract relating to the Project; (g) changes in market conditions, electricity prices, renewable energy credit prices, or the economic viability of the Project; or (h) any other event, circumstance, or condition, whether or not foreseeable, that may affect Tenant\'s ability or willingness to perform its obligations under this Lease. Tenant hereby irrevocably and unconditionally waives any and all rights it may have at law, in equity, or under any statute (including without limitation California Civil Code Sections 1932 and 1933) to terminate, rescind, or cancel this Lease for any of the foregoing reasons or for any other reason not expressly set forth in this Lease.

**[ARTICLE 16 --- CONDEMNATION]{.underline}**

**Section 16.1 --- Total Taking**

In the event of a total taking of the Premises by eminent domain, condemnation, or inverse condemnation, or a conveyance in lieu thereof (a \"**Total Taking**\"), this Lease shall terminate as of the date on which title to the Premises vests in the condemning authority or the date on which the condemning authority takes physical possession of the Premises, whichever occurs first; *provided, however*, that Tenant\'s obligation to pay Rent and all other monetary obligations under this Lease shall continue through the date of such termination, and Tenant shall not be entitled to any refund or credit for Rent previously paid. Landlord shall be entitled to receive and retain the entire condemnation award or proceeds arising from the Total Taking, and Tenant shall have no claim to, or interest in, any portion of Landlord\'s award. Tenant may, however, make a separate claim directly against the condemning authority for the value of Tenant\'s Improvements and for Tenant\'s relocation expenses, provided that such separate claim does not diminish, offset, or otherwise reduce the award payable to Landlord.

**Section 16.2 --- Partial Taking**

21	**Purpose.** The purpose of this playbook is to establish internal benchmarks for negotiating ground leases for utility-scale solar photovoltaic generation facilities, with a primary focus on California markets. The geographic markets of principal concern include Kern County, Los Angeles County, Riverside County, San Bernardino County, and Imperial County, each of which presents distinct land-use, permitting, and pricing dynamics. This playbook is intended to serve as the authoritative internal reference document for all REP personnel and outside counsel engaged in the negotiation, review, and execution of solar ground lease agreements.
22	
23	**Scope.** This playbook covers all material lease provisions for projects of 50 MW nameplate capacity and above. The guidance herein is applicable to both single-axis tracker and fixed-tilt photovoltaic configurations, though single-axis tracker installations (which represent the substantial majority of REP\'s current pipeline) may involve slightly higher per-acre land requirements due to tracker row spacing and may accordingly affect the per-acre rent analysis.
24	
25	**Reference Comparable.** The Antelope Ridge Solar Project lease (200 MW, Lancaster, California; executed March 8, 2022) serves as the primary executed comparable for California ground lease terms throughout this playbook. Antelope Ridge was negotiated by REP\'s legal team with outside counsel support from Whitfield, Crane & Polk LLP, financed by Cascade Western Capital LLC, and represents a fully bankable lease structure that was accepted without material modification by the lender\'s counsel. Where other comparables are relevant, they are noted; however, the Antelope Ridge lease should be treated as the baseline reference for all California ground lease negotiations.
26	
27	**Organization.** This playbook is organized by provision category. Each category presents a \"Market Standard\" (representing the most commonly observed and preferred market terms across REP\'s portfolio and comparable industry transactions) and an \"Acceptable Range\" (representing the outer boundary of terms that REP can accept without escalation). Each provision also includes a \"Lender Bankability\" notation based on Cascade Western Capital LLC\'s requirements. Provisions marked **\"REQUIRED\"** must be present for project finance closing; provisions marked **\"PREFERRED\"** are strongly recommended but may be negotiable with a lender waiver.
28	
29	**Escalation Protocol.** Any proposed lease that deviates from the \"Acceptable Range\" set forth in this playbook requires escalation to the General Counsel for approval before term sheet or letter of intent execution. This escalation requirement applies regardless of the commercial attractiveness of the project site or the urgency of the development timeline.
30	
31	**Total Land Cost Benchmark.** Market standard for total annual land cost --- encompassing all forms of rent, including fixed rent, variable or percentage rent, option period rent, and any other payments to the landlord --- should not exceed 5% to 8% of projected annual project revenue. Any lease structure that would cause total annual land cost to exceed 8% of projected annual revenue triggers a mandatory financial review by the Development and Finance teams and requires General Counsel approval before further negotiation.
32

34	
35	**[Market Standard]{.underline}**
36	
37	**Initial Term.** The market standard initial lease term for utility-scale solar ground leases in California is 30 to 35 years from the Commencement Date. The preferred initial term is 35 years, which provides a 15-year operational tail beyond the expiration of a typical 20-year power purchase agreement (\"PPA\"), allowing the developer to capture residual and merchant-tail value during the post-PPA period.
38	
39	**Extension Options.** Two (2) five-year extension terms, exercisable at Tenant\'s sole and absolute option upon written notice delivered no less than 12 months prior to the expiration of the then-current term. Extension options must be exercisable unilaterally by the Tenant without requiring the Landlord\'s consent.
40	
41	**Total Potential Term.** 40 to 45 years (30-year initial term plus two 5-year extensions at the minimum; 35-year initial term plus two 5-year extensions at the maximum).
42	
43	**Extension Rent.** Fair Market Value (\"FMV\") as determined by a mutually agreed independent MAI-certified appraiser, subject to a floor equal to the annual rent payable in the final year of the immediately preceding term and a cap of 110% of such final-year rent. This floor-and-cap structure ensures that the landlord receives at least the prior rent level while preventing unreasonable rent increases during extension periods.
44	
45	**[Acceptable Range]{.underline}**
46	
47	**Initial Term.** Not less than 30 years; 35 years is strongly preferred to provide an adequate operational and merchant tail beyond a typical 20-year PPA term. An initial term shorter than 30 years is below market, creates financing risk, and requires General Counsel escalation.
48	
49	**Extension Options.** A minimum of two 5-year options is required. As an alternative, one 10-year option is acceptable, provided it is exercisable unilaterally by the Tenant. Extension options requiring mutual consent of both Landlord and Tenant are not acceptable --- a mutual-consent \"option\" is not a true option and is functionally meaningless for financing purposes, as it gives the Landlord an effective veto over the Tenant\'s ability to extend and therefore provides no certainty to the project finance lender.
50	
51	**Total Potential Term.** Not less than 40 years. A total potential term (including all extensions) of less than 40 years is below market and will require significant additional analysis to determine whether the project\'s financial model can support the truncated term.
52	
53	**Extension Rent.** FMV with mutual appraiser selection. Single-party appraiser selection (e.g., an appraiser selected solely by the Landlord) is not acceptable, as it introduces the potential for biased valuation and eliminates the Tenant\'s ability to ensure a fair market determination.
54	
55	**[Lender Bankability (Cascade Western Capital)]{.underline}**
56	
57	**REQUIRED.** Cascade Western Capital requires that the minimum lease term --- including all extension options exercisable unilaterally by the Tenant --- must exceed the loan maturity date by at least 5 years. For a typical 20-year PPA with an 18-year term loan, the lease must extend to at least 23 years beyond Commercial Operation Date (\"COD\"), and preferably 25 or more years beyond COD. A lease with a total potential term shorter than the PPA term plus the debt amortization period will not be financed. Mutual-consent extensions are not counted toward the minimum lease term for lender underwriting purposes because they are not within the Tenant\'s (or lender\'s) control.
58	
59	**[Rationale and Notes]{.underline}**
60	
61	A 20-year PPA from COD (for example, Q2 2027 through Q2 2047) requires a lease extending to at least 2050--2052 to capture residual and merchant tail value during the post-PPA period. Extension options must be \"bankable\" --- meaning the lender can rely on them being exercised if needed to protect the project\'s long-term revenue stream. Mutual-consent extensions give the landlord a veto and therefore provide no certainty to the lender, who will disregard them entirely in its underwriting analysis.
62	
63	The Antelope Ridge comparable lease (executed March 8, 2022) had a 35-year initial term with two 5-year extensions (total potential term of 45 years), exercisable unilaterally by the Tenant, with extension rent determined at FMV by a mutually agreed MAI-certified appraiser subject to a floor/cap mechanism.
64	
65	**[Section 3: Rent Structure]{.underline}**
66	
67	**[Section 3.1: Option Period Rent]{.underline}**
68	
69	**Market Standard.** Option period rent of \$40 to \$75 per acre per year during the pre-construction development period is within the current market range for California desert and agricultural sites. The option period typically runs for 24 to 36 months from lease execution, during which the developer completes permitting, interconnection studies, environmental review, and financing activities.
70	
71	**Acceptable Range.** Up to \$100 per acre per year is acceptable in high-demand areas or where the landlord has competing offers from other developers. The option period should not exceed 36 months from execution. If the developer requires additional time, the option may include one or two 12-month extension rights at the same or modestly increased per-acre rate.
72	
73	**Lender Bankability.** Option period rent is not typically a focus of the project finance lender, as it is a pre-financing cost borne by the developer\'s equity during the development phase.
74	
75	**Notes.** Option period rent compensates the landowner for tying up the property and foregoing alternative uses while the developer completes its pre-construction activities. For a 1,240-acre site at \$50 per acre, option period rent would total approximately \$62,000 per year --- a modest and entirely reasonable carrying cost during the development phase.
76	
77	**[Section 3.2: Base Rent (Fixed Rent)]{.underline}**
78	
79	**Market Standard.** Base rent for Kern County and comparable California desert and agricultural regions ranges from \$800 to \$1,100 per acre per year. This range reflects market conditions observed across REP\'s portfolio and comparable transactions since 2020.
80	
81	**Acceptable Range.** \$800 to \$1,100 per acre per year for the initial period (Years 1 through 10 or Years 1 through 15, depending on the lease structure). If the lease includes a step-up in base rent for subsequent periods, the stepped-up rate should remain within the \$800 to \$1,100 per acre per year market range. A mid-term step-up that causes the per-acre rate to exceed the market ceiling --- for example, an increase to \$1,350 per acre per year --- is above-market and requires escalation to the General Counsel.
82	
83	**Flat vs. Step-Up Structure.** Step-ups in base rent between defined periods are an accepted market structure, provided the rates at each step remain within the applicable market range. Landlords may request step-ups to account for the time value of money or to approximate inflation adjustments without a formal escalation mechanism. Such requests are reasonable and negotiable, provided the resulting per-acre rate does not breach the market ceiling at any point during the lease term.
84	
85	**Notes.**
86	
87	> • For a 1,240-acre site, base rent at the market midpoint (\$950 per acre) totals \$1,178,000 per year; at the top of the range (\$1,100 per acre) the total is \$1,364,000 per year.
88	>
89	> • Kern County rates have been relatively stable at \$800 to \$1,100 per acre since 2020. Agricultural lease alternatives for fallow dryland in the region range from \$100 to \$250 per acre, so the solar premium is substantial and provides meaningful economic incentive for landowners to execute solar ground leases.
90	>
91	> • The Antelope Ridge comparable lease (Lancaster, California) had base rent of \$950 per acre per year, applied as a flat rate for the entire initial term with no mid-term step-up.
92	
93	**Lender Bankability.** The lender models rent as a fixed operating expense in its debt service coverage ratio (\"DSCR\") analysis. Above-market rent directly reduces the project\'s DSCR and may require the developer to contribute additional equity to meet minimum coverage thresholds. Cascade Western Capital\'s standard underwriting model is calibrated to market-range rent; above-market rent will be flagged in the lender\'s credit review.
94	
95	**[Section 3.3: Revenue Share / Percentage Rent]{.underline}**
96	
97	**Market Standard.** Revenue share (also referred to as \"percentage rent\") is either (a) not included in the lease, or (b) used as an alternative to fixed rent --- not in addition to fixed rent. The majority of recent California utility-scale solar ground leases in REP\'s experience use a fixed-rent-only structure with no revenue share component.
98	
99	**Acceptable Range.**
100	
101	> • **If no revenue share:** Fixed rent only within the range specified in Section 3.2.
102	>
103	> • **If revenue share is used as an alternative to fixed rent:** 1.0% to 2.0% of net revenue, defined as gross revenue less curtailment payments, grid charges, and applicable taxes. Revenue share calculated on gross revenue (i.e., without deduction for curtailment and grid charges) is not acceptable. The distinction between gross and net revenue is critical because curtailment events and grid charges within the California Independent System Operator (\"CAISO\") market can reduce net revenue by 5% to 15% relative to gross revenue, particularly during periods of solar over-generation.
104	>
105	> • **Additive structure:** A lease structure that includes both fixed rent and a revenue share component (i.e., fixed rent plus percentage rent) is not market standard and is not acceptable without General Counsel approval. Such an additive structure creates a \"double-dip\" that inflates total land cost well above the 5% to 8% rent-to-revenue target established in Section 1 of this playbook.
106	
107	**Lender Bankability.** Revenue share provisions, if present, must be subordinated to debt service or, at minimum, structured so that total rent (fixed plus variable) does not impair the project\'s DSCR below 1.30x at any point during the loan term. Cascade Western Capital\'s standard project finance term sheet requires that total site lease cost (including all forms of rent) not exceed 8% of P50 projected annual revenue.
108	
109	**Notes.**
110	
111	> • The Antelope Ridge comparable lease had no revenue share component. Rent was structured as fixed rent only at \$950 per acre per year with 2.0% simple annual escalation.
112	>
113	> • Illustration of the impact of an additive structure: For a project generating \$14.45 million in annual PPA revenue, a 3.5% gross revenue share would equal \$505,750 per year. Combined with base rent of \$1,364,000 per year (i.e., 1,240 acres at \$1,100 per acre), total annual rent would be \$1,869,750 --- representing 12.94% of annual project revenue. This is far in excess of the 5% to 8% target and would be flagged as a material credit concern by any project finance lender.
114	
115	**[Section 3.4: Escalation]{.underline}**
116	
117	**Market Standard.** Annual rent escalation of 1.5% to 2.0%, applied on a simple (non-compounding) basis. Simple escalation means that the escalation percentage is applied to the original base rent amount each year, rather than to the prior year\'s escalated rent.
118	
119	**Acceptable Range.** 1.5% to 2.0% simple escalation. Compounding escalation (where the escalation percentage is applied to the prior year\'s rent, producing geometric growth) is not acceptable without General Counsel approval. Compounding escalation at rates above 2.0% is specifically disfavored and has been flagged by Cascade Western Capital as a material credit concern.
120	
121	**Compounding vs. Simple --- Impact Analysis.** The difference between simple and compounding escalation is modest in the early years but becomes highly material over the life of a long-term ground lease. The following analysis illustrates the divergence:
122	
123	> • **Simple escalation at 2.0% over 25 years:** Year 25 rent = Base Rent × (1 + 0.02 × 24) = Base Rent × 1.48 --- representing a 48% increase from Year 1 to Year 25.
124	>
125	> • **Compounding escalation at 2.0% over 25 years:** Year 25 rent = Base Rent × (1.02)\^24 = Base Rent × 1.608 --- representing a 60.8% increase from Year 1 to Year 25.
126	>
127	> • **Compounding escalation at 3.0% over 25 years:** Year 25 rent = Base Rent × (1.03)\^24 = Base Rent × 2.033 --- representing a 103.3% increase from Year 1 to Year 25. Under this structure, rent effectively doubles by Year 25.
128	>
129	> • The difference between 2.0% simple escalation and 3.0% compounding escalation over a 25-year term results in a cumulative overpayment of approximately 55% of the simple-escalation total --- a massive and entirely avoidable cost differential.
130	
131	**Lender Bankability.** Lenders model rent escalation against fixed PPA revenue. In a typical fixed-price PPA (the dominant structure in the California market), the \$/MWh price is fixed for the PPA term with no escalator. Compounding escalation at rates above 2.0% therefore creates a \"scissors effect\" in which rent grows faster than revenue, progressively reducing the project\'s DSCR over time and potentially causing a covenant breach in the later years of the loan term. Cascade Western Capital has flagged compounding escalation above 2.0% as a material credit concern in its standard project finance term sheet, and the lender\'s credit committee may require a rent reserve account or additional equity cushion to mitigate the risk.
132	
133	**Notes.**
134	
135	> • The Antelope Ridge comparable lease used 2.0% simple annual escalation applied to the original base rent amount, consistent with the market standard described above.
136	>
137	> • PPA counterparties (such as Pacific Basin Energy Corp., a frequent California offtaker) typically offer fixed \$/MWh pricing with no escalator or, at most, a 1.0% annual escalator. Therefore, any rent escalation mechanism that exceeds general inflation (\~2.0%) creates progressive margin compression over the lease term, reducing the project\'s net operating income and equity returns year over year.
138	
139	**[Section 4: Commencement Date]{.underline}**
140	
141	**Market Standard.** The Commencement Date should be defined as the later of (a) the date of Commercial Operation (\"COD\") as defined under the Tenant\'s PPA, or (b) a date certain providing sufficient construction runway, typically 36 months after lease execution. This structure ensures that fixed rent obligations do not commence until the project is generating revenue, while providing the landlord with a backstop date by which rent will begin regardless of project status.
142	
143	**Acceptable Range.**
144	
145	> • COD-triggered commencement is strongly preferred and is the market-standard approach for utility-scale solar ground leases.
146	>
147	> • If a date-certain backstop is required by the landlord, it should be no earlier than 36 months after execution. This timeline accounts for the interconnection queue delays, permitting contingencies, environmental review processes, and supply chain disruptions that are common in the current California solar development environment.
148	>
149	> • The \"earlier of\" formulation (i.e., the Commencement Date is the earlier of COD or X months after execution) is acceptable only if X is equal to or greater than 36 months. A backstop of 24 months or less is too aggressive for California solar projects given current CAISO interconnection queue timelines, which routinely extend 3 or more years for cluster study completion and system upgrade processes.
150	
151	**Construction Commencement Deadlines.** Many landlord-form leases include a separate deadline by which the Tenant must commence construction activities on the premises, with the landlord retaining a right to terminate the lease if the deadline is not met. The market standard for such a deadline is 24 to 30 months from execution, with extension rights if delays are caused by interconnection queue processing, permitting authority delays, or force majeure events. An 18-month construction commencement deadline with no extension rights and no force majeure carve-outs is unreasonably tight and creates significant termination risk for the developer.
152	
153	**Lender Bankability (Cascade Western Capital).** **REQUIRED.** The lender requires that the lease Commencement Date is tied to COD or provides a backstop of at least 36 months from execution. Early rent triggers that cause fixed rent obligations to accrue before COD impair the project\'s ability to service construction loan interest, create negative carry during the construction phase, and reduce the available equity contribution. Cascade Western Capital will not finance a project where the ground lease triggers rent obligations materially in advance of revenue generation.
154	
155	**Notes.**
156	
157	> • The Antelope Ridge comparable lease defined the Commencement Date as the earlier of COD or 36 months after execution. Construction was required to commence within 30 months of execution, with automatic 12-month extensions for interconnection queue delays and force majeure events, and the lease was executed with a fully bankable Commencement Date structure.
158	>
159	> • CAISO interconnection cluster studies are currently experiencing processing timelines of 36 to 48 months from application to completion. A 24-month backstop date could therefore trigger rent obligations well before the project has received its interconnection approval and can begin construction, let alone achieve COD and begin generating revenue. This risk is not speculative --- it reflects the current reality of the CAISO queue.
160	
161	**[Section 5: Security Deposit]{.underline}**
162	
163	**Market Standard.** The market standard security instrument is a standby letter of credit (\"LOC\") issued by a creditworthy financial institution (typically a bank with a minimum credit rating of A- from S&P or equivalent), in an amount equal to 6 to 12 months of Year 1 base rent. For a project with Year 1 base rent of \$1,364,000, this translates to a security deposit range of \$682,000 to \$1,364,000.
164	
165	**Acceptable Range.**
166	
167	> • **Form:** LOC is strongly preferred. Cash deposits are not acceptable in the ordinary course due to (a) the cash trap imposed on developer liquidity during the construction and early-operation phases, (b) landlord insolvency risk (if the landlord becomes insolvent, the cash deposit may be treated as the landlord\'s asset rather than the tenant\'s), and (c) the lost interest and opportunity cost of tying up project capital in a non-productive deposit.
168	>
169	> • **Amount:** 6 months minimum, 12 months maximum of Year 1 base rent. A security deposit of \$3,000,000 against Year 1 base rent of \$1,364,000 represents approximately 26 months of rent --- more than double the market maximum and a significant over-collateralization of the landlord\'s exposure.
170	>
171	> • **Interest:** If a cash deposit is accepted in extraordinary circumstances (e.g., the Tenant is unable to obtain an LOC from a qualifying institution), the deposit must be held in an interest-bearing account at a federally insured financial institution, with all interest accruing to the Tenant.
172	>
173	> • **Reduction:** The security amount should be reduced by 50% after COD and the achievement of 6 consecutive months of commercial operation without a Tenant default event. This reduction mechanism is standard and reflects the fact that the landlord\'s risk exposure decreases significantly once the project is operational and generating revenue.
174	>
175	> • **Return:** The full remaining security balance should be returned to the Tenant within 30 days of lease expiration or termination, less any amounts properly applied by the Landlord to cure documented and uncured Tenant defaults.
176	
177	**Lender Bankability.** An LOC is the preferred instrument from the lender\'s perspective because it does not reduce the project\'s available cash for construction. A \$3,000,000 cash deposit would reduce available equity by approximately 1.5% of a \$198 million project capital cost --- a material impact during the construction phase when every dollar of equity is allocated to specific construction milestones and contingency reserves.
178	
179	**Notes.**
180	
181	> • The Antelope Ridge comparable lease required an LOC equal to 9 months\' base rent (approximately \$675,000, based on Antelope Ridge\'s base rent of \$950 per acre per year), reduced to 6 months\' base rent after COD and 6 consecutive months of default-free commercial operation.
182	>
183	> • Cash security deposits held in non-interest-bearing accounts are particularly disfavored because the landlord bears no carrying cost for holding the Tenant\'s capital, creating a perverse incentive to maximize the deposit amount and resist reduction or return.
184	
185	**[Section 6: Assignment and Transfer]{.underline}**
186	
187	**[Market Standard]{.underline}**
188	
189	Landlord consent is required for assignment of the lease, such consent not to be unreasonably withheld, conditioned, or delayed. The following categories of transfers are \"permitted transfers\" that do not require Landlord consent:
190	
191	> \(a\) Transfers to Tenant\'s affiliates (i.e., entities under common control with Tenant, where \"common control\" means direct or indirect ownership of 50% or more of the voting equity interests);
192	>
193	> \(b\) Transfers to a project finance lender (or its designee or nominee) as collateral security, or upon foreclosure, exercise of remedies, or deed-in-lieu of foreclosure;
194	>
195	> \(c\) Transfers in connection with a sale of all or substantially all of Tenant\'s assets or equity interests, including tax equity financing transactions, mergers, consolidations, and similar corporate reorganizations.
196	
197	**Change of Control.** Changes in the direct or indirect ownership of entities above the project-entity level (i.e., upstream parent entities, holding companies, and fund vehicles) should not constitute an \"assignment\" under the lease and should not trigger consent requirements. Solar project entities are typically structured as special purpose vehicles (\"SPVs\") that are owned by multi-layered holding company and fund structures; ownership changes at the parent, fund, or investor level are routine occurrences (particularly in connection with tax equity syndications and secondary market sales) and should not require landlord consent or notification.
198	
199	**Post-Assignment Liability.** Upon a permitted assignment to a creditworthy assignee that assumes all obligations under the lease, the original Tenant should be released from further liability under the lease. Continuing joint-and-several liability of the original Tenant after assignment is not market standard and is problematic because, in a project finance structure, the original Tenant SPV may be dissolved, recapitalized, or converted into a holding entity with no operating assets following a permitted transfer.
200	
201	**[Acceptable Range]{.underline}**
202	
203	> • The \"not unreasonably withheld, conditioned, or delayed\" standard is the minimum acceptable consent standard. A \"sole and absolute discretion\" consent standard is never acceptable in a project finance context, as it gives the landlord an unconstrained veto over any transfer --- including transfers to the project finance lender upon foreclosure --- and effectively renders the project unfinanceable.
204	>
205	> • A \"reasonableness\" standard that includes specific, objective conditions for the exercise of reasonableness (e.g., the assignee must meet a minimum net worth threshold of \$10 million or demonstrate creditworthiness commensurate with the remaining lease obligations) is acceptable and, in some cases, may provide greater certainty than an unqualified \"reasonableness\" standard.
206	>
207	> • At minimum, affiliate transfers and lender/foreclosure transfers must be carved out from consent requirements. The asset-sale/equity-sale carve-out is strongly preferred but may be negotiable if the reasonableness standard is sufficiently robust.
208	
209	**[Lender Bankability (Cascade Western Capital)]{.underline}**
210	
211	**REQUIRED.** The lender must have the right to (a) take a leasehold mortgage or deed of trust on the Tenant\'s leasehold interest as security for the project financing, (b) assign the lease to a purchaser at a foreclosure sale or to the lender itself (or its designee) without landlord consent, or at minimum with landlord consent not to be unreasonably withheld, and (c) designate a new tenant following foreclosure or deed-in-lieu of foreclosure, provided such new tenant assumes all obligations under the lease. A \"sole and absolute discretion\" consent standard is a deal-breaker for project finance. Upstream change-of-control triggers that would require landlord consent for ownership changes above the project-entity level are likewise incompatible with standard project finance structures and will not be accepted by Cascade Western Capital.
212	
213	**[Notes]{.underline}**
214	
215	> • The Antelope Ridge comparable lease included all three permitted transfer carve-outs (affiliate, lender, and asset/equity sale) and used a \"not unreasonably withheld, conditioned, or delayed\" consent standard for all other assignments. No upstream change-of-control trigger was included. The original Tenant was released from liability upon assignment to a creditworthy successor that assumed all lease obligations.
216	>
217	> • Joint-and-several continuing liability is particularly problematic in the context of tax equity financing transactions, where the original Tenant SPV may be restructured as part of a partnership flip or inverted lease pass-through transaction.
218	
219	**[Section 7: Lender Protections (Estoppel, SNDA, Leasehold Mortgagee Rights)]{.underline}**
220	
221	**[Market Standard]{.underline}**
222	
223	The lease must include the following five provisions as a condition to bankability. These provisions are non-negotiable requirements of Cascade Western Capital LLC and substantially all other institutional project finance lenders.
224	
225	> **(a) Estoppel Certificates.** Landlord must deliver estoppel certificates within 15 business days of the Tenant\'s or lender\'s written request. Each estoppel certificate must certify the current status of the lease, including confirmation that the lease is in full force and effect, that rent is current through a specified date, that no defaults exist (or, if defaults exist, specifying the nature of such defaults), and such other matters as the lender may reasonably request.
226	>
227	> **(b) Subordination, Non-Disturbance, and Attornment (SNDA).** Landlord must enter into a subordination, non-disturbance, and attornment agreement in a form reasonably acceptable to the lender, confirming that the lease will survive any foreclosure of a superior lien on the fee interest (including any existing or future mortgage, deed of trust, or other encumbrance on the landlord\'s fee estate). The SNDA ensures that the Tenant\'s leasehold interest --- and by extension, the lender\'s security interest in the leasehold --- is not extinguished by a foreclosure action against the landlord.
228	>
229	> **(c) Leasehold Mortgagee Cure Rights.** The lender must receive copies of all default notices simultaneously with the Tenant and must have independent cure rights with a 60-day cure period for monetary defaults and a 90-day cure period for non-monetary defaults, in each case running from the date the lender receives the default notice. If the cure of a non-monetary default requires the lender to obtain possession of the premises (through foreclosure or deed-in-lieu), the lender must have additional time to complete the foreclosure process --- typically 180 days --- before the landlord may exercise termination rights.
230	>
231	> **(d) Lender Recognition / New Tenant.** Landlord must recognize a new tenant designated by the lender following foreclosure, deed-in-lieu of foreclosure, or other exercise of remedies, provided such new tenant assumes all obligations under the lease. The landlord may not refuse to recognize the new tenant on the basis of the predecessor tenant\'s defaults that have been cured by the lender.
232	>
233	> **(e) Cooperation with Financing.** Landlord must cooperate reasonably with the Tenant\'s efforts to obtain project financing, including executing consents, certificates, acknowledgments, and other documents reasonably requested by the lender or its counsel in connection with the closing of any project financing. This cooperation obligation should not impose material costs on the Landlord; the Tenant should reimburse the Landlord\'s reasonable, documented out-of-pocket expenses (including attorney\'s fees) incurred in connection with such cooperation.
234	
235	**[Acceptable Range]{.underline}**
236	
237	All five provisions are required. There is no acceptable range --- the absence of any of these provisions is a deal-breaker for project finance and will require a complete redraft of the relevant lease sections.
238	
239	**[Lender Bankability (Cascade Western Capital)]{.underline}**
240	
241	**REQUIRED.** These provisions are non-negotiable conditions to financing. A lease that is entirely silent on lender protections --- containing no estoppel obligation, no SNDA commitment, no leasehold mortgagee cure rights, no lender recognition provisions, and no cooperation clause --- is not financeable and will require a complete redraft.
242	
243	**[Notes]{.underline}**
244	
245	> • The Antelope Ridge comparable lease included all five provisions. The estoppel turnaround period was 15 business days. Lender cure periods were 60 days (monetary) and 90 days (non-monetary) with a 180-day foreclosure extension. The SNDA was executed simultaneously with the lease closing and project financing closing.
246	>
247	> • Landlord\'s counsel may be unfamiliar with these provisions if they lack experience in renewable energy or project finance transactions. In such cases, education and explanation of the purpose and mechanics of each provision may be necessary and appropriate. REP\'s legal team and outside counsel should be prepared to provide model language and explanatory memoranda to facilitate landlord\'s counsel\'s review.
248	
249	**[Section 8: Default and Cure Periods]{.underline}**
250	
251	**[Market Standard]{.underline}**
252	
253	**Monetary Defaults.** Thirty (30) calendar days\' written notice and opportunity to cure, measured from the date the Tenant receives written notice specifying the nature and amount of the monetary default. The cure period does not commence until written

The lender\'s cure periods run concurrently with (or following, as applicable) the Tenant\'s cure periods and are not extinguished by the Tenant\'s failure to cure.
