7	**[Acceptable Range]{.underline}**
8	
9	> • **Monetary:** Not less than 30 days from written notice. A cure period of 15 calendar days is unacceptable under any circumstances.
10	>
11	> • **Non-Monetary:** Not less than 60 days from written notice, with extension rights for defaults that are not reasonably capable of cure within 60 days. A 30-day non-monetary cure period without extension rights is the absolute floor and should be accepted only in extraordinary circumstances with General Counsel approval.
12	>
13	> • A lease that provides a uniform cure period for all defaults (i.e., the same period for both monetary and non-monetary defaults) should, at minimum, distinguish between the two categories and provide longer cure periods for non-monetary defaults, which are inherently more complex to remediate.
14	
15	**[Lender Bankability (Cascade Western Capital)]{.underline}**
16	
17	**REQUIRED.** Cascade Western Capital insists on minimum cure periods of 30 days for monetary defaults and 60 days for non-monetary defaults for the Tenant, plus the lender\'s own independent cure periods of 60 days (monetary) and 90 days (non-monetary) with an additional foreclosure extension of up to 180 days. A cure period of 15 calendar days is entirely incompatible with project finance --- it is insufficient for the lender to even receive and process a default notice, engage counsel, and initiate a wire transfer.
18	
19	**[Notes]{.underline}**
20	
21	> • The Antelope Ridge comparable lease provided 30 days for monetary defaults and 60 days (extendable to 180 days) for non-monetary defaults, with lender cure periods of 60 days (monetary) and 90 days (non-monetary) plus a 180-day foreclosure extension.
22	>
23	> • As a practical matter, 15 calendar days may be insufficient even to identify a billing error, verify the landlord\'s calculations, process internal approvals, and execute a wire transfer. This concern is particularly acute where the default notice is sent by U.S. Mail rather than email or overnight delivery, as mail transit adds 5 to 7 days to the effective cure period.
24	
25	**[Section 9: Termination Rights]{.underline}**
26	
27	**[Section 9.1: Landlord Termination Rights]{.underline}**
28	
29	**Market Standard.** The Landlord may terminate the lease only upon the Tenant\'s uncured material default, subject to the cure periods specified in Section 8 and the lender\'s independent cure rights specified in Section 7. In no event may the Landlord terminate the lease if the lender is diligently pursuing a cure within the lender\'s applicable cure period (including any foreclosure extension period).
30	
31	**Construction Commencement Deadline.** Many landlord-form leases include a right for the Landlord to terminate if the Tenant fails to commence construction within a specified period. The market standard for such a deadline is 24 to 30 months from lease execution, with automatic extensions for interconnection queue delays, permitting delays, and force majeure events of not less than 12 months in the aggregate. An 18-month construction commencement deadline without any extension rights or force majeure carve-outs is unacceptable, as it does not account for the realities of the current California permitting and interconnection environment.
32	
33	**Acceptable Range.** Construction commencement deadline of not less than 24 months, with at least 12 months of cumulative extension rights for interconnection delays, permitting delays, and force majeure events.
34	
35	**Notes.** The Landlord\'s right to terminate for failure to commence construction must include appropriate carve-outs for delays beyond the Tenant\'s reasonable control, including CAISO interconnection queue delays, local permitting authority processing times, environmental review and mitigation requirements, and supply chain disruptions.
36	
37	**[Section 9.2: Tenant Termination Rights]{.underline}**
38	
39	**Market Standard.** The Tenant must have the right to terminate the lease in the following circumstances:
40	
41	> **(a) Condemnation.** If eminent domain or condemnation proceedings affect more than 25% of the leased premises or materially impair the design, construction, or operation of the solar generation facility, the Tenant may terminate the lease upon written notice to the Landlord.
42	>
43	> **(b) Extended Force Majeure.** If a force majeure event continues for more than 365 consecutive days and prevents the construction or operation of the solar generation facility, the Tenant may terminate the lease upon written notice to the Landlord.
44	>
45	> **(c) Change in Law / Regulatory Change.** If a change in applicable federal, state, or local law, regulation, ordinance, or governmental action renders the solar generation facility economically unviable or illegal to construct or operate, the Tenant may terminate the lease upon written notice to the Landlord.
46	
47	**Acceptable Range.** All three tenant termination triggers are market standard and should be present in every utility-scale solar ground lease. The absence of any tenant termination rights is a significant deviation from market practice and should be escalated to the General Counsel.
48	
49	**Lender Bankability.** Tenant termination rights are important for lender protections. If the project becomes economically unviable or physically impossible to operate, the lender needs the Tenant to be able to exit the lease, recover and redeploy the project equipment (the lender\'s collateral), and mitigate losses --- rather than being locked into a non-performing lease obligation that drains cash from a non-operating project.
50	
51	**Notes.**
52	
53	> • The Antelope Ridge comparable lease included all three tenant termination rights with the following thresholds: 25% of premises (condemnation), 365 consecutive days (force majeure), and an economic viability test (change in law). Each termination right was subject to a 60-day advance written notice period.
54	>
55	> • A lease with no tenant termination rights effectively converts the site lease into a take-or-pay obligation regardless of whether the project can operate. This creates an asymmetric risk profile that is fundamentally incompatible with project finance.
56	
57	**[Section 9.3: Improvements Upon Termination]{.underline}**
58	
59	**Market Standard.** Upon termination --- whether by expiration of the lease term, Landlord default, or Tenant default --- the Tenant retains ownership of all improvements (including the solar generation facility, racking systems, inverters, transformers, balance-of-system equipment, access roads, and related infrastructure) and has the right (and obligation) to remove such improvements during the decommissioning period. Improvements should never automatically vest in the Landlord upon Tenant\'s default. The solar generation facility is the Tenant\'s property at all times, and the Landlord\'s remedies upon default are limited to the remedies specified in the default and termination provisions of the lease.
60	
61	**Acceptable Range.** A provision granting the Landlord the option to require the Tenant to abandon improvements in place (as an alternative to removal) is an acceptable and, in some cases, commercially reasonable accommodation --- some landlords may prefer to retain the facility infrastructure for future use or repowering by a successor developer. However, a provision that automatically forfeits ownership of the solar generation facility and all improvements to the Landlord, without compensation, upon the occurrence of a Tenant default is never acceptable. Such a forfeiture provision is economically confiscatory, creates a perverse incentive for the Landlord to provoke or allege defaults, and would be challenged as an unenforceable penalty under California law.
62	
63	**Lender Bankability (Cascade Western Capital).** **REQUIRED.** The solar generation facility is the lender\'s primary collateral, along with the PPA revenue stream. A forfeiture clause that transfers ownership of a \$198 million facility to the Landlord upon a Tenant default would wipe out the lender\'s collateral in its entirety and is an absolute deal-breaker. Cascade Western Capital will not lend into any lease that contains a forfeiture-of-improvements provision, and no waiver or workaround is available for this requirement.
64	
65	**Notes.**
66	
67	> • The Antelope Ridge comparable lease provided that the Tenant retains ownership of all improvements at all times during and after the lease term. Upon expiration or termination, the Tenant has the obligation to remove all improvements within 18 months. The Landlord may elect, in its sole discretion, to require the Tenant to leave some or all improvements in place, in which case the Tenant\'s removal obligation is waived with respect to such improvements.
68	>
69	> • A forfeiture provision also creates a deeply perverse incentive structure: if the Landlord can seize a fully operational, revenue-generating solar facility by alleging a default (even a minor or technical default), the Landlord stands to gain an asset worth tens or hundreds of millions of dollars in exchange for nothing. This incentive is contrary to the fundamental purpose of the ground lease relationship and would generate significant litigation risk.
70	
71	**[Section 10: Decommissioning and Site Restoration]{.underline}**
72	
73	**Market Standard.**
74	
75	> • **Security Amount:** A surety bond or letter of credit equal to 100% of the estimated decommissioning cost, as determined by a licensed professional engineer.
76	>
77	> • **Timing of Posting:** The decommissioning security is posted no earlier than Year 10 of the initial term, reflecting the fact that decommissioning liability is a long-dated obligation that does not arise until the end of the project\'s operational life. Early posting imposes unnecessary cost on the project during the construction and early-operation phases.
78	>
79	> • **Cost Estimate:** The estimated decommissioning cost is determined by a licensed professional engineer mutually agreed upon by the Landlord and the Tenant. The estimate is updated every 5 years to account for changes in removal technology, labor costs, salvage values, and regulatory requirements.
80	>
81	> • **Removal Timeline:** 12 to 18 months after lease expiration or termination to complete removal of all improvements and restoration of the site to its pre-project condition (or such other condition as may be specified in the lease).
82	>
83	> • **Failure Penalty:** If the Tenant fails to complete removal within the allotted period, the Landlord may complete removal at the Tenant\'s expense, with the Tenant responsible for actual documented costs plus a 10% administrative fee.
84	
85	**Acceptable Range.**
86	
87	> • **Security:** 100% of estimated cost. Up to 110% may be acceptable if other lease terms are favorable and the landlord\'s justification is reasonable. A requirement of 150% of estimated cost is excessive and not market.
88	>
89	> • **Timing:** Year 10 at the earliest. Year 15 is acceptable and, in some cases, preferred. A Year 5 posting deadline is too early and imposes unnecessary cost during the construction and ramp-up phase, when project cash flow is most constrained.
90	>
91	> • **Cost Estimate:** The estimate must be determined by a mutually agreed professional engineer. Sole determination by the Landlord\'s consultant --- for example, an engineering firm selected unilaterally by the Landlord without Tenant input --- creates a conflict of interest and the potential for inflated cost estimates. The Tenant must have the right to participate in the selection of the engineer and to review and comment on the cost estimate.
92	>
93	> • **Timeline:** Not less than 12 months. A 6-month removal timeline is insufficient for the decommissioning of a utility-scale solar facility, which involves disconnection from the grid, de-energization, removal of hundreds of thousands of panels, racking, piles, electrical infrastructure, access roads, and site grading and restoration.
94	>
95	> • **Failure Penalty:** Actual documented cost plus a 10% to 15% administrative premium is market. A 200% liquidated damages multiplier (i.e., the Landlord may charge twice the actual cost of removal as a penalty) is punitive, is likely unenforceable as a penalty clause under California Civil Code Section 1671, and is not consistent with market practice.
96	
97	**Lender Bankability.** The lender reviews decommissioning terms to ensure they do not create early-term cash traps or disproportionate liabilities that impair the project\'s cash flow or debt service capacity. A Year 5 posting deadline with a 150% bond requirement could impair project cash flow during the critical early-operation years and may trigger covenant concerns in the lender\'s financial model.
98	
99	**Notes.**
100	
101	> • The Antelope Ridge comparable lease required a bond at 100% of estimated decommissioning cost, posted at Year 10, with costs determined by a mutually agreed licensed professional engineer, an 18-month removal period, and an actual-cost-plus-10% penalty for late removal.
102	>
103	> • Typical decommissioning costs for utility-scale solar installations range from \$30,000 to \$50,000 per MW. For a 150 MW project, this translates to an estimated decommissioning cost of \$4.5 million to \$7.5 million. At 150% of the high estimate, the required security would be \$11.25 million --- a significant additional financial burden, particularly if posted at Year 5 when the project may still be in the early stages of debt repayment.
104	
105	**[Section 11: Access and Operations]{.underline}**
106	
107	**[Section 11.1: Landlord Access to Premises]{.underline}**
108	
109	**Market Standard.** The Landlord may access the leased premises for inspection purposes upon reasonable prior written notice of no less than 48 hours, except in the case of a bona fide emergency (fire, flood, imminent structural failure, or other circumstances posing an immediate threat to life or property) where access may be immediate and without prior notice. In all cases, the Landlord and any visitors or invitees of the Landlord must comply with the Tenant\'s site safety protocols.
110	
111	**Acceptable Range.**
112	
113	> • Minimum 48 hours\' written notice for routine inspections. In extraordinary circumstances, 24 hours\' notice may be acceptable if accompanied by robust safety protocol requirements.
114	>
115	> • All visitors, including the Landlord and the Landlord\'s agents, contractors, and invitees, must comply with the Tenant\'s site safety protocols, including personal protective equipment (\"PPE\") requirements, electrical safety clearance procedures, and restricted-area access rules.
116	>
117	> • The Landlord must be accompanied by a Tenant representative during any site visit. Unaccompanied access is not acceptable.
118	
119	**Safety and Regulatory Considerations.** An energized solar generation facility operates at voltages ranging from 600V DC at the module string level to 34.5kV AC at the point of interconnection. Unrestricted and unannounced access to such a facility creates serious personal injury risk for the landlord, potential OSHA liability for the Tenant (as the facility operator and employer of record), and potential violations of the National Electrical Code (\"NEC\") and National Fire Protection Association (\"NFPA\") standards. Market standard requires that all non-essential personnel (including the landowner) follow lockout/tagout (\"LOTO\") procedures when entering restricted areas and be escorted by qualified Tenant personnel at all times.
120	
121	**Notes.**
122	
123	> • The Antelope Ridge comparable lease required 48 hours\' written notice except in genuine emergencies, with the Landlord required to comply with all site safety rules and regulations and accompanied by a Tenant representative at all times during site visits.
124	>
125	> • Unannounced landlord access to an energized solar facility is not merely a commercial preference --- it is a material safety concern that implicates federal and state workplace safety regulations.
126	
127	**[Section 11.2: Agricultural Operations and Mineral Rights]{.underline}**
128	
129	**Agricultural Operations.** No agricultural operations of any kind are permitted within the leased premises during the lease term. Dust generated by tilling and harvesting, irrigation runoff, pesticide drift, and mechanical activity from concurrent agricultural operations can damage solar panels, reduce generation efficiency by 2% to 5% over the panel warranty period, create accelerated degradation and maintenance liabilities, and void manufacturer warranties in some cases. The entire leased premises --- including setback areas, access corridors, drainage easements, and buffer zones --- must be under the Tenant\'s exclusive operational control for the duration of the lease.
130	
131	**Mineral Rights.** The Landlord may retain mineral rights underlying the leased premises, but such retention must be subject to a \"no surface use\" covenant. Under a \"no surface use\" covenant, the Landlord (and any mineral lessee, licensee, or assignee claiming through the Landlord) may not conduct any surface activities --- including drilling, grading, excavation, hydraulic fracturing, seismic testing, construction of access roads, staging of equipment, or any other surface disturbance --- on or within the boundaries of the leased premises during the lease term. Subsurface extraction from adjacent parcels is permitted only if it does not cause surface subsidence, vibration, groundwater contamination, or other interference with the Tenant\'s solar operations.
132	
133	**Acceptable Range.**
134	
135	> • **Agricultural:** Complete prohibition of agricultural operations within the premises is required. Co-use arrangements (also known as \"agrivoltaic\" configurations) may be appropriate for certain small-scale community solar installations but are not acceptable for utility-scale solar projects of 50 MW and above due to operational complexity, equipment compatibility concerns, and panel soiling and damage risks.
136	>
137	> • **Mineral:** A \"no surface use\" covenant is the minimum acceptable standard. In geographies with active subsurface mineral extraction (such as Kern County, which has extensive oil and gas production), the Tenant should also have a right to review and approve (such approval not to be unreasonably withheld) any subsurface mineral extraction plan that could affect the leased premises, including plans for extraction from adjacent parcels where the extraction activities could cause subsidence, vibration, or other physical effects on the solar facility.
138	>
139	> • An unrestricted reservation of mineral lease rights --- allowing the Landlord to grant third-party mineral leases without restriction, including the right of such mineral lessees to conduct surface operations within the solar facility --- is a material operational risk and is not market for utility-scale solar ground leases.
140	
141	**Lender Bankability.** The lender requires that nothing in the lease permits third-party activity on the leased premises that could interfere with project operations, damage the lender\'s collateral (the solar generation facility), or impair the project\'s ability to generate revenue and service debt. Unrestricted mineral rights and concurrent agricultural operations are both unacceptable from the lender\'s perspective.
142	
143	**Notes.**
144	
145	> • The Antelope Ridge comparable lease included a comprehensive \"no surface use\" covenant for mineral rights and prohibited all agricultural activity within the leased premises for the duration of the lease term.
146	>
147	> • Kern County is one of the most active oil and gas production regions in California, and mineral rights issues are particularly relevant in this geography. Many parcels in Kern County have severed mineral estates, and the interaction between solar ground leases and pre-existing mineral interests requires careful due diligence and drafting attention.
148	
149	**[Section 12: Insurance Requirements]{.underline}**
150	
151	**Market Standard.** The Tenant is required to maintain the following insurance coverages throughout the lease term:
152	
153	> • **Commercial General Liability (\"CGL\"):** \$5 million to \$10 million per occurrence, with an aggregate limit of \$10 million to \$20 million.
154	>
155	> • **Property / Builder\'s Risk Insurance:** Full replacement cost of the solar generation facility, including all improvements, equipment, and infrastructure installed on the leased premises.
156	>
157	> • **Pollution Liability Insurance:** \$5 million to \$10 million per occurrence. Pollution liability coverage is increasingly standard for utility-scale solar projects, reflecting the growing integration of battery energy storage system (\"BESS\") components (which contain lithium-ion cells and thermal management fluids), transformer oil and dielectric fluids, and construction-phase soil disturbance and stormwater management obligations.
158	>
159	> • **Landlord as Additional Insured:** The Landlord must be named as an additional insured on the CGL and property insurance policies. The Landlord should also receive certificates of insurance upon request and 30 days\' advance written notice of any material change, cancellation, or non-renewal of coverage.
160	>
161	> • **Self-Insurance:** Self-insurance is permitted if the Tenant (or its parent guarantor) meets minimum net worth and credit rating thresholds, typically \$500 million in net tangible assets or an investment-grade credit rating (BBB- or higher from S&P, Baa3 or higher from Moody\'s).
162	
163	**Acceptable Range.** CGL limits up to \$10 million per occurrence and \$20 million aggregate are within market for projects of 100 MW and above. Pollution liability limits up to \$10 million are within market. A prohibition on self-insurance is negotiable but is not a material deviation for most project-entity tenants that do not independently meet the net worth or credit rating thresholds.
164	
165	**Notes.** Insurance requirements in the \$10 million/\$20 million range are standard and well-established for utility-scale solar generation facilities and should not be flagged as excessive or above-market. Pollution liability requirements reflect industry trends toward battery storage integration and the increasing regulatory focus on construction-phase environmental compliance.
166	
167	**[Section 13: Miscellaneous Provisions]{.underline}**
168	
169	**[Section 13.1: Quiet Enjoyment]{.underline}**
170	
171	**Market Standard.** The Landlord covenants that the Tenant shall have quiet enjoyment of the leased premises for the entire lease term (including all extension periods), free from interference, disturbance, or molestation by the Landlord or any person or entity claiming by, through, or under the Landlord. This covenant runs with the land and is binding on the Landlord\'s successors and assigns.
172	
173	**[Section 13.2: Recording]{.underline}**
174	
175	**Market Standard.** The Tenant has the right to record a memorandum of lease (in a form mutually agreed upon by the parties) in the office of the county recorder for the county in which the leased premises are located. The Landlord must cooperate with the preparation and recording of the memorandum of lease, including executing and acknowledging the memorandum in recordable form. The memorandum of lease provides constructive notice to third parties of the Tenant\'s leasehold interest and is essential for title insurance and lender security purposes.
176	
177	**[Section 13.3: Condemnation]{.underline}**
178	
179	**Market Standard.** If more than 25% of the leased premises are taken by eminent domain or condemnation proceedings, the Tenant may terminate the lease upon written notice to the Landlord, as set forth in Section 9.2(a) above. The condemnation award is allocated between the Landlord (for the value of the fee interest in the taken property) and the Tenant (for the value of the leasehold interest, the solar generation facility, and all improvements), with each party having the right to participate independently in the condemnation proceedings and to make a separate claim for its respective interest.
180	
181	**[Section 13.4: Hazardous Materials]{.underline}**
182	
183	**Market Standard.** The Tenant is responsible for the proper handling, storage, use, and disposal of any hazardous materials introduced to the leased premises by the Tenant or its agents, contractors, or subcontractors. The Landlord is responsible for any pre-existing contamination on the leased premises that predates the commencement of the Tenant\'s activities. A baseline environmental assessment (Phase I ESA, and Phase II if warranted) is strongly recommended prior to lease execution to establish the pre-existing environmental condition of the premises and to allocate responsibility clearly between the parties.
184	
185	**[Section 13.5: Governing Law and Dispute Resolution]{.underline}**
186	
187	**Market Standard.** The lease is governed by the laws of the State of California. Disputes arising under the lease are resolved by binding arbitration administered by JAMS or a comparable arbitration provider, or by litigation in the Superior Court of the State of California for the County of Kern (or the county in which the leased premises are located). Each party bears its own attorneys\' fees and costs unless the lease provides otherwise.
188	
189	**[Appendix A: Summary Comparison Table]{.underline}**
190	
191	The following table provides a quick-reference summary of the market standards and acceptable ranges for each material lease provision addressed in this playbook.
192	
193	  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
194	  **\#**            **Provision**                **Market Standard**                                                       **Acceptable Range**
195	  ----------------- ---------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------- -----------------------------------------------------------------------
196	  1                 Initial Term                 30--35 years                                                              Not less than 30 years
197	
198	  2                 Extension Options            Two 5-year options, Tenant unilateral                                     Minimum two options, Tenant unilateral; one 10-year option acceptable
199	
200	  3                 Total Potential Term         40--45 years                                                              Not less than 40 years
201	
202	  4                 Base Rent                    \$800--\$1,100/acre/year                                                  \$800--\$1,100/acre/year; no mid-term step-up above range
203	
204	  5                 Revenue Share                None, or 1%--2% of net revenue as alternative to fixed rent               Not additive to fixed rent; not calculated on gross revenue
205	
206	  6                 Escalation                   1.5%--2.0% simple (non-compounding)                                       1.5%--2.0% simple; no compounding without GC approval
207	
208	  7                 Total Rent as % of Revenue   5%--8% of projected annual revenue                                        Not to exceed 8%
209	
210	  8                 Commencement Date            COD or 36-month backstop                                                  Not less than 36-month backstop
211	
212	  9                 Security Deposit             LOC, 6--12 months\' Year 1 base rent                                      LOC; \$682K--\$1,364K range; no cash deposits
213	
214	  10                Assignment                   Not unreasonably withheld; 3 carve-outs (affiliate, lender, asset sale)   No sole discretion; lender carve-out required at minimum
215	
216	  11                Lender Protections           Estoppel, SNDA, cure rights, lender recognition, cooperation              All five required; no acceptable omission
217	
218	  12                Cure Periods                 30 days monetary / 60 days non-monetary with extension                    Minimum 30 days monetary / 60 days non-monetary
219	
220	  13                Tenant Termination Rights    Condemnation (25%), FM (365 days), change in law                          All three required
221	
222	  14                Improvements on Default      Tenant retains ownership at all times                                     No forfeiture clause permitted
223	
224	  15                Decommissioning Security     100% of estimated cost, posted Year 10, mutual engineer                   Not \>110%; not before Year 10; mutual engineer required
225	
226	  16                Decommissioning Timeline     12--18 months for removal                                                 Not less than 12 months
227	
228	  17                Decommissioning Penalty      Actual documented cost + 10% administrative fee                           Not \>15% premium; no punitive multipliers
229	
230	  18                Agricultural Operations      Prohibited within premises                                                Complete prohibition required
231	
232	  19                Mineral Rights               Retained with \"no surface use\" covenant                                 \"No surface use\" covenant required at minimum
233	
234	  20                Landlord Access              48 hours\' written notice except emergency                                Not less than 24 hours; escort required
235	
236	  21                Insurance (CGL)              \$5M--\$10M per occ. / \$10M--\$20M aggregate                             Up to \$10M/\$20M acceptable
237	
238	  22                Option Period Rent           \$40--\$75/acre/year                                                      Up to \$100/acre/year
239	  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
240	
241	**[Appendix B: Cascade Western Capital LLC --- Key Lease Requirements Summary]{.underline}**
242	
243	The following is a summary of Cascade Western Capital LLC\'s non-negotiable lease requirements, extracted from their standard project finance term sheet (last updated June 2024) and confirmed through discussions with Cascade Western Capital\'s project finance team (lead contact: Daniel Ortiz, Managing Director, Project Finance). These requirements apply to all solar ground leases securing projects financed by Cascade Western Capital.
244	
245	> • **Minimum Lease Term.** The total lease term, including all extension options exercisable unilaterally by the Tenant, must exceed the loan maturity date by at least 5 years. Mutual-consent extensions are not counted.
246	>
247	> • **Assignment / Lender Foreclosure Transfers.** The lease must permit assignment to the lender (or its designee) upon foreclosure, deed-in-lieu of foreclosure, or other exercise of remedies, without landlord consent or with consent not to be unreasonably withheld.
248	>
249	> • **Estoppel Certificates.** The landlord must be obligated to deliver estoppel certificates within 15 business days of the Tenant\'s or lender\'s written request.
250	>
251	> • **Subordination, Non-Disturbance, and Attornment.** The landlord must execute an SNDA in a form reasonably acceptable to the lender, confirming that the lease survives any foreclosure of a superior lien on the fee interest.
252	>
253	> • **Lender Cure Rights.** The lender must receive copies of all default notices and must have independent cure rights: 60 days for monetary defaults, 90 days for non-monetary defaults, plus additional time (up to 180 days) to complete foreclosure if necessary to effectuate a cure.
254	>
255	> • **Lender Recognition of Successor Tenant.** The landlord must recognize a new tenant designated by the lender post-foreclosure, provided such new tenant assumes all lease obligations.
256	>
257	> • **No Forfeiture of Improvements.** Under no circumstances may the lease provide for forfeiture of the solar generation facility (the lender\'s primary collateral) to the landlord upon tenant default. This is an absolute, non-waivable requirement.
258	>
259	> • **Total Site Lease Cost.** Total site lease cost (including all forms of rent --- fixed, variable, escalated, and any other payments to the landlord) must not exceed 8% of P50 projected annual revenue.
260	>
261	> • **No Third-Party Interference.** The lease must not permit any third-party activity on the leased premises (including agricultural operations or surface mineral extraction) that could damage or interfere with the lender\'s collateral or the project\'s ability to generate revenue.
262	>
263	> • **Cooperation Clause.** The landlord must be obligated to cooperate reasonably with the Tenant\'s financing efforts, including executing consents, certificates, and other documents reasonably requested by the lender in connection with project financing closing.
264

**[CASCADE WESTERN CAPITAL LLC]{.underline}**

**Standard Site Lease Requirements for Renewable Energy Project Finance**

*Excerpt from Construction-to-Term Loan Facility --- Indicative Term Sheet*

CONFIDENTIAL --- For Discussion Purposes Only

This document is provided by Cascade Western Capital LLC, a New York limited liability company (\"Lender\"), in connection with preliminary financing discussions for utility-scale renewable energy projects. This document is current as of August 2024 and supersedes all prior versions.

The following sets forth Cascade Western Capital LLC\'s (\"Lender\") minimum requirements for site control documents (ground leases, easements, and related agreements) securing real property upon which a financed renewable energy project is to be constructed and operated. These requirements are conditions precedent to closing and funding of any construction-to-term loan facility. Failure of a site lease to satisfy these requirements will require modification of the lease or provision of alternative credit support acceptable to Lender in its sole discretion.

**[1. Minimum Lease Term and Extension Options]{.underline}**

**1.1 Minimum Initial Term.** The site lease must have an initial term of not less than the longer of (a) the full term of the power purchase agreement (\"PPA\") plus five (5) years, or (b) thirty (30) years from the projected commercial operation date (\"COD\"). For a project with a 20-year PPA, this requires a minimum initial term of 25 years from COD (not from lease execution), though Lender\'s strong preference is for initial terms of 30--35 years from COD. The initial term must be measured from COD, and any gap period between lease execution and COD must not consume term that is required for debt service coverage.

**1.2 Extension Options.** The site lease must include not fewer than two (2) extension terms of five (5) years each, exercisable at the sole option of the tenant (borrower) upon written notice to landlord delivered not less than twelve (12) months prior to the expiration of the then-current term. Extension options requiring landlord consent or mutual agreement are not acceptable to Lender because they do not provide certainty of site control through the full debt amortization period. Each extension option must be independently exercisable, and the exercise of the first extension option must not be a condition precedent to the exercise of the second.

**1.3 Total Minimum Term.** Lender requires a total potential lease term (initial term plus all extension options) of not less than forty (40) years. A total potential term of less than forty (40) years will require additional credit support or accelerated amortization schedules, which may adversely impact project economics and borrower returns. A total potential term of forty-five (45) years or greater is preferred and consistent with market practice for utility-scale solar and storage projects.

**1.4 Debt Amortization Alignment.** Lender\'s standard construction-to-term loan facilities contemplate debt amortization schedules of up to twenty-two (22) years following COD, and the site lease must remain in effect (inclusive of unilateral extension options) for the full amortization period plus a minimum tail period of three (3) years. Any shortfall in lease term relative to the amortization schedule plus tail period will require structural modifications to the loan, including but not limited to shortened amortization, cash sweep mechanisms, or additional collateral.

**1.5 Extension Rent.** Extension term rent must be determinable by formula or fixed escalation. Fair market value resets determined solely by landlord\'s appraiser are not acceptable. If fair market value (\"FMV\") is used as a component of extension rent, the determination must be made by a mutually agreed independent appraiser with demonstrable experience in renewable energy ground leases, and the extension rent must be subject to a cap equal to the greater of (x) the rent payable in the final year of the immediately preceding term and (y) fair market value for comparable solar ground leases in the relevant market.

**[2. Assignment, Transfer, and Change of Control]{.underline}**

**2.1 General Standard.** The site lease must provide that landlord\'s consent to assignment or subletting shall not be unreasonably withheld, conditioned, or delayed. A consent standard of \"sole and absolute discretion\" is not acceptable to Lender. The lease must expressly state that landlord\'s consent is subject to a reasonableness standard and must identify objective criteria, if any, upon which landlord may base a refusal.

**2.2 Permitted Transfers (No Consent Required).** The lease must include carve-outs from the consent requirement for the following transfers, which must be permitted without landlord consent and without payment of any transfer fee, premium, or additional consideration:

> \(a\) **Affiliate Transfers.** Assignments or transfers to any entity that directly or indirectly controls, is controlled by, or is under common control with, the tenant (borrower), where \"control\" means the direct or indirect ownership of fifty percent (50%) or more of the voting interests of such entity;
>
> \(b\) **Lender Transfers / Collateral Assignments.** Assignments of the leasehold interest as collateral security in connection with any project financing, and any transfer to Lender (or its designee, nominee, or transferee) upon exercise of remedies under the loan documents, including foreclosure, deed-in-lieu, UCC sale, or other enforcement actions;
>
> \(c\) **Transfers in Connection with Acquisition.** Transfers in connection with a sale of all or substantially all of the tenant\'s assets or the project assets, including any merger, consolidation, or reorganization of the tenant;
>
> \(d\) **Tax Equity Transfers.** Transfers to or among tax equity investors or their affiliates in connection with the project\'s tax equity financing structure, including flip transactions, buyouts, and put/call exercises.

**2.3 Upstream Change of Control.** Changes in the direct or indirect ownership of the tenant above the project-entity level (including changes in ownership of the tenant\'s parent, sponsor, managing member, general partner, or fund investors) must not constitute an \"assignment\" or trigger any landlord consent requirement. Lender requires this carve-out because project finance loans are typically made to special-purpose project entities, and upstream ownership changes---including fund transfers, sponsor recapitalizations, limited partner transfers, and secondary market transactions---are routine and must not jeopardize site control.

**2.4 Release of Original Tenant.** Upon a permitted assignment where the assignee assumes all obligations under the lease, the original tenant must be released from further liability under the lease. Continuing joint-and-several liability of the original tenant post-assignment is not acceptable in project finance structures, as it creates credit uncertainty, complicates enforcement, and may give rise to intercreditor issues.

**2.5 Notice Only.** For all permitted transfers described in Section 2.2, tenant shall provide landlord with written notice within thirty (30) days after the effective date of the transfer, but no prior consent shall be required. The notice shall identify the transferee and include evidence that the transfer qualifies as a permitted transfer.

**[3. Estoppel Certificates, SNDA, and Leasehold Mortgagee Protections]{.underline}**

**3.1 Estoppel Certificates.** Landlord must be obligated to deliver a signed estoppel certificate within fifteen (15) business days of tenant\'s or Lender\'s written request. The estoppel certificate must confirm: (i) that the lease is in full force and effect and has not been modified (or identifying all modifications); (ii) the current rent and any other amounts due; (iii) whether any defaults exist on the part of either party (and if so, specifying the nature and details of such defaults); (iv) the remaining term and applicable extension options; (v) that no offsets, credits, or claims exist against rent; and (vi) such other matters as Lender may reasonably request. Failure to deliver the estoppel within such fifteen (15) business day period shall be deemed landlord\'s confirmation that no defaults exist, the lease is in full force and effect, and all statements contained in the form of estoppel delivered by tenant or Lender are true and correct.

**3.2 Subordination, Non-Disturbance, and Attornment (SNDA).** Landlord must execute and deliver, within fifteen (15) business days of request, an SNDA agreement in form and substance reasonably acceptable to Lender. The SNDA must provide that: (i) landlord\'s fee interest is subordinate to Lender\'s leasehold mortgage or deed of trust; or, alternatively, if landlord\'s fee interest is senior, the SNDA must include non-disturbance protections ensuring the lease survives any foreclosure of the fee interest; (ii) Lender (or its transferee, designee, or purchaser at foreclosure sale) will be recognized as tenant under the lease following any foreclosure or exercise of remedies; and (iii) Lender shall not be liable for any acts or omissions of any prior tenant except to the extent such obligations are continuing obligations that first arise after Lender or its designee takes possession of the premises.

**3.3 Leasehold Mortgagee Protections (Lender Cure Rights).** The site lease must include the following protections for Lender as leasehold mortgagee:

> \(a\) Landlord must deliver to Lender a copy of any notice of default or termination simultaneously with delivery to tenant, at an address specified by Lender from time to time by written notice;
>
> \(b\) Lender must have the right (but not the obligation) to cure any tenant default under the lease on behalf of tenant;
>
> \(c\) Lender\'s cure period must be not less than sixty (60) days after the expiration of tenant\'s cure period for monetary defaults, and not less than ninety (90) days after the expiration of tenant\'s cure period for non-monetary defaults;
>
> \(d\) If the non-monetary default is of a nature that cannot be cured without obtaining possession of the premises (e.g., through foreclosure or the appointment of a receiver), Lender\'s cure period must be extended for such additional time as is reasonably necessary for Lender to commence and complete foreclosure proceedings or other enforcement actions, provided Lender is diligently pursuing such proceedings and is curing all monetary defaults during such extended period;
>
> \(e\) Landlord may not terminate the lease or exercise any remedy with respect to the leasehold estate without first providing Lender written notice and an opportunity to cure in accordance with the periods described above; and
>
> \(f\) Upon foreclosure or other exercise of remedies by Lender, Lender (or its designee) must be recognized as tenant under the lease, and if the existing lease is terminated for any reason, landlord must enter into a new lease with Lender (or its designee) on substantially the same terms and conditions as the terminated lease, for the remainder of the then-applicable term.

**3.4 Financing Cooperation.** Landlord must agree to reasonably cooperate with tenant\'s financing activities, including executing consents, certificates, acknowledgments, and other documents reasonably requested by Lender in connection with the project financing, at no cost to landlord (other than landlord\'s own counsel fees, which tenant shall reimburse upon request). Landlord\'s failure or refusal to cooperate with financing activities within the time periods specified herein shall constitute a material default by landlord under the lease.

**[4. Default and Cure Periods]{.underline}**

**4.1 Minimum Tenant Cure Periods.** The site lease must provide the following minimum cure periods for tenant defaults before landlord may exercise termination or other remedies:

> \(a\) **Monetary Defaults.** Not less than thirty (30) days\' written notice from landlord, specifying the nature and amount of the monetary default. Landlord may not impose late fees, penalties, or interest during the initial thirty-day cure period.
>
> \(b\) **Non-Monetary Defaults.** Not less than sixty (60) days\' written notice from landlord, specifying the nature of the non-monetary default with reasonable particularity. If the non-monetary default is of a nature that cannot reasonably be cured within sixty (60) days, the cure period must be extended for such additional time as is reasonably necessary, provided tenant has commenced cure within the initial sixty-day period and is diligently pursuing cure to completion.

**4.2 Lender Cure Rights (Cross-Reference).** In addition to tenant\'s cure periods set forth above, Lender must receive the additional cure periods described in Section 3.3 of this document. Landlord may not terminate the lease or exercise any termination remedy unless both tenant\'s and Lender\'s respective cure periods have expired without the applicable default having been cured.

**4.3 Minimum Cure Periods --- Rationale.** Cure periods of less than thirty (30) days for monetary defaults and sixty (60) days for non-monetary defaults are not acceptable to Lender because they do not afford Lender sufficient time to (i) receive notice of the default, (ii) evaluate the nature and scope of the default, (iii) determine whether to exercise cure rights or pursue alternative remedies, and (iv) if necessary, commence foreclosure proceedings or other enforcement actions to protect Lender\'s collateral position.

**4.4 No Automatic Termination.** The lease must not contain any provision for automatic termination upon the occurrence of an event of default, the passage of time, or any other triggering event. All termination of the lease must be subject to the notice and cure procedures described in this Section 4 and the leasehold mortgagee protections described in Section 3.3.

**[5. Collateral Protections --- Improvements and Equipment]{.underline}**

**5.1 Tenant Ownership of Improvements.** The site lease must confirm that all improvements, equipment, fixtures, and personal property installed by tenant on the premises---including without limitation solar panels, racking and tracker systems, inverters, transformers, electrical collection systems, battery energy storage system (\"BESS\") components, substation equipment, meteorological stations, fencing, access roads, and all related infrastructure---remain the personal property of tenant (and, by extension, the collateral of Lender) at all times during the lease term and upon expiration or termination of the lease.

**5.2 No Forfeiture of Improvements.** Under no circumstances may the lease provide that tenant\'s improvements become the property of landlord upon default, termination, expiration, or any other event. Any such forfeiture provision would constitute a destruction of Lender\'s collateral and is absolutely unacceptable. For a utility-scale solar or solar-plus-storage project with capital costs in excess of one hundred million dollars (\$100,000,000), a forfeiture provision creates an unjust windfall to landlord, eliminates Lender\'s recovery on its primary collateral, and renders the project unfundable. This prohibition applies regardless of the characterization of such provision as a \"liquidated damages\" clause, a \"security interest,\" or otherwise.

**5.3 Right to Remove.** Tenant (and Lender as assignee, successor, or designee) must have the right to remove all improvements and equipment from the premises upon expiration or termination, subject to reasonable decommissioning obligations as described in Section 6 below.

**5.4 Lender\'s Right of Access.** Upon any default, termination, or expiration, Lender (and its agents, contractors, and designees) must have the right to access the premises for a period of not less than twelve (12) months to disassemble, remove, and transport all project equipment and improvements constituting Lender\'s collateral. This right of access must survive the termination or expiration of the lease and must be enforceable against landlord and any successor to landlord\'s interest.

**5.5 UCC Fixture Filing.** Landlord must consent to the filing of UCC financing statements (including fixture filings) with respect to tenant\'s equipment and improvements, and must acknowledge that such items are and shall remain personal property of tenant and are not fixtures of the real property. Landlord must further agree not to claim any landlord\'s lien, right of distraint, or similar interest in tenant\'s equipment or improvements.

**[6. Additional Lease Requirements (Summary)]{.underline}**

The following additional requirements apply to all site leases securing financed renewable energy projects. These requirements are summarized below and may be further specified in the definitive loan documents:

> • **Memorandum of Lease.** The lease must be recorded, or a memorandum thereof must be recorded, in the official real property records of the county where the premises are located, at or prior to loan closing. The memorandum must identify the lease term, extension options, and the existence of Lender\'s leasehold mortgage.
>
> • **Quiet Enjoyment.** The lease must include landlord\'s covenant of quiet enjoyment, ensuring tenant\'s peaceful and undisturbed use and possession of the premises for the full initial term and all extension terms, free from interference by landlord or any party claiming through landlord.
>
> • **Insurance.** Tenant must maintain insurance as reasonably required under the lease; however, landlord\'s insurance requirements must not impose limitations on self-insurance programs maintained by investment-grade-rated entities or their affiliates. Specific insurance coverage amounts and types are project-dependent and will be addressed in the definitive loan documents.
>
> • **Security Deposit / Letter of Credit.** Lender prefers that any lease security required by landlord be in the form of a standby letter of credit rather than a cash deposit. Cash deposits held by landlord create credit risk to Lender if landlord becomes insolvent and the deposit is commingled with landlord\'s general assets. If a cash security deposit is required, it must be held in a segregated, interest-bearing escrow account at a financial institution acceptable to Lender, and Lender must have a perfected security interest in such deposit.
>
> • **Decommissioning Obligations.** Decommissioning security must be reasonable in amount (not exceeding one hundred percent (100%) of estimated net decommissioning costs as determined by a mutually agreed independent engineer, taking into account salvage value), posted at a reasonable time (not earlier than Year 10 of the initial term), and removal timelines following expiration or termination must be not less than twelve (12) months.
>
> • **Landlord Representations.** Landlord must represent and warrant: (a) fee simple title to the premises free of encumbrances that would interfere with the project; (b) authority to enter into the lease; (c) no conflicts with other agreements; and (d) no pending condemnation proceedings, environmental claims, or liens affecting the premises.
>
> • **Force Majeure / Condemnation.** The lease must include tenant termination rights in the event of (a) condemnation or taking affecting more than twenty-five percent (25%) of the premises or rendering the project commercially unviable, (b) force majeure events continuing for more than three hundred sixty-five (365) consecutive days, or (c) a change in law rendering the project unlawful or economically unviable.
>
> • **Surface Use Restrictions.** If landlord retains mineral rights or any reversionary agricultural rights, the lease must include a \"no surface use\" covenant prohibiting any mineral extraction, drilling, or related activity on the surface of the premises that could interfere with project operations, transmission, or access. Landlord must not retain or exercise rights to conduct agricultural operations, grazing, or any other surface activities on the leased premises during the lease term that are inconsistent with the project\'s operations and maintenance requirements.

**[7. General Disclaimer and Closing]{.underline}**

The foregoing requirements represent Lender\'s minimum standards for site control documents in connection with renewable energy project financings. Lender reserves the right to impose additional or modified requirements based on the specific characteristics of the project, the creditworthiness of the borrower and its sponsors, the terms of the applicable power purchase agreement, and the particular provisions of the site lease under review.

Any site lease that does not comply with the requirements set forth herein will require modification as a condition precedent to closing and funding. Lender strongly recommends that borrowers share these requirements with landlords and their counsel early in the lease negotiation process to avoid delays in financing.

Questions regarding these requirements may be directed to Cascade Western Capital LLC\'s Real Estate Counsel.

This document does not constitute a commitment to lend, an offer to finance, or an agreement to provide credit on any terms. Any financing is subject to satisfactory completion of credit approval, due diligence, environmental review, independent engineer review, legal review, and negotiation and execution of definitive loan documents satisfactory to Lender in all respects.
